value.title: nginx — Full-detail knowledge graph
value.description: A source-grounded, machine-readable graph of nginx, its features, protocols, architecture, ecosystem, history, licensing, comparative notes and implementation considerations.
value.scope: Based on the user-provided Wikipedia article text. Inferences are explicitly labeled.

value.name: Edge reverse proxy
value.description: Clients connect to nginx, which terminates or handles HTTP-level traffic and forwards requests to upstream application services.
value.source_basis: Core reverse-proxy role is explicit; detailed deployment flow is a generalized architecture interpretation.

value.name: Static content delivery
value.description: nginx serves static files, index files and optionally auto-indexed directory listings.

value.name: Load-balanced application
value.description: nginx distributes incoming requests across backend servers and can use in-band health checks.
value.source_basis: Load balancing and in-band health checks are explicitly listed.

value.name: Reverse proxy with HTTP caching
value.description: nginx caches eligible responses so repeated requests can be served without always querying the backend.
value.source_basis: Caching is explicit; exact cache policy and bypass rules are not covered in the supplied article.

value.name: Dynamic application integration
value.description: nginx serves as a front end for dynamic content through FastCGI, SCGI, uWSGI, WSGI application servers or Phusion Passenger.

value.name: TLS-enabled frontend
value.description: nginx supports TLS/SSL features such as SNI, OCSP stapling and TLS protocol integrations; a frontend TLS termination topology is a common inference.
value.source_basis: TLS/SSL features are explicit; exact termination topology is inferred.

value.name: Mail protocol proxy
value.description: nginx can proxy SMTP, POP3 and IMAP, with TLS/SSL and STARTTLS; authentication is delegated to an external HTTP server or script.
value.source_basis: Protocol and authentication features are explicit.

value.name: Graceful configuration or executable upgrade
value.description: The article states nginx can upgrade its executable and configuration without losing client connections.
value.source_basis: Explicitly listed feature; operational procedure is not detailed in the supplied article.

value.name: Containerized web frontend
value.description: nginx is commonly deployed in Docker containers according to a 2018 usage survey; container orchestration details are outside the source.
value.source_basis: The source reports a historical survey finding, not a current universal deployment statistic.

value.name: Commercial API gateway and management
value.description: NGINX Plus API gateway functionality was associated with NGINX Controller, announced as an API management tool in 2017.
value.source_basis: Commercial product relationship is explicit; flow is conceptual.

value.rule: For high numbers of concurrent connections, nginx's asynchronous event-driven approach is a core architectural choice.
value.rationale: The article contrasts its event-driven model with thread-based handling and connects it to predictable performance under high load.

value.rule: Do not assume nginx natively supports Apache-style .htaccess per-file overrides.
value.rationale: The article explicitly identifies this as a flexibility difference.

value.rule: Verify third-party module compatibility and build requirements before deploying modules.
value.rationale: The article notes modules may need to be compiled alongside nginx, may not all support dynamic loading, and some still require static linking.

value.rule: Treat the article's HTTP/3 status as experimental from nginx 1.25.0, not as a blanket statement about every build or later release.
value.rationale: The source specifically characterizes HTTP/3 as experimental starting with version 1.25.0.

value.rule: Encrypted Client Hello support depends on using a compatible OpenSSL branch and the relevant nginx build/configuration.
value.rationale: The source conditions ECH support on nginx 1.29.4 and an OpenSSL branch implementing ECH.

value.rule: Plan an external HTTP service or authentication script for nginx mail-proxy authentication.
value.rationale: The source says mail proxy authentication requires an external HTTP server or script.

value.rule: Do not assume NGINX Unit receives upstream maintenance after October 2025.
value.rationale: The article says it was archived by maintainers and is no longer receiving updates.

value.rule: Distinguish the BSD-licensed nginx project from proprietary NGINX Plus.
value.rationale: The source lists different license models.

value.rule: When relying on native ACME automation, verify the deployed nginx version and certificate lifecycle configuration.
value.rationale: The article reports native ACME issuance and renewal support, but does not provide a complete configuration procedure.

value.rule: Keep popularity figures tied to the survey and date rather than treating them as timeless market share.
value.rationale: The article cites different survey dates and populations, including all websites versus the busiest sites.

value.rule: Define cacheability, invalidation, and bypass rules explicitly when using nginx HTTP caching.
value.rationale: The source confirms reverse-proxy caching but does not describe policy details; this is an implementation recommendation inferred from the capability.

value.rule: Consider upstream health checks when deploying nginx as a load balancer.
value.rationale: In-band health checks are listed as a load-balancing feature.

value.rule: Describe the 2019 Rambler matter as a reported copyright claim/dispute, not as a settled determination of ownership.
value.rationale: The supplied article describes allegations and subsequent events but does not establish a court finding that resolves ownership.

value.rule: Validate protocol features against the exact nginx version and build in use.
value.rationale: The article ties multiple capabilities to particular versions and build dependencies.

value.rule: Treat versions, adoption statistics, and project status as claims from the supplied article snapshot, not independently verified current facts.
value.rationale: The article contains dated and potentially time-sensitive claims.

value.label: Image vs physical disc
value.description: Image is a transferable binary artifact; physical disc is the optical medium it represents.

value.label: Mount vs burn
value.description: Mount exposes image through an OS interface; burning creates physical optical media.

value.label: Archival vs emulation
value.description: The same image artifact can preserve disc contents or provide input to an emulator.

value.label: ISO vs virtual CD-ROM
value.description: ISO is the stored image; virtual CD-ROM is the runtime interface exposing it as optical media.

value.label: Filesystem binary copy vs raw media copy
value.description: ISO preserves filesystem/user data rather than every physical-media control/error structure.

value.label: Track addressing vs file addressing
value.description: Audio CD content is addressed through track/index/time structures rather than filesystem files.

source_claims.text: Optical disc image is a sector-by-sector disk image containing disc filesystem and data.
Images can be created from optical discs, file collections, or other image files.
ISO stores user data, not control headers/error correction; logical data sectors are 2,048 bytes.
An image can be transferred over data links/removable media unlike a physical optical disc.
Suitable driver software can expose ISO to the OS as though it were a physical optical disc.
ISO has no physical track concept and cannot fully represent multi-track discs.
Audio CDs cannot be represented as ISO because audio tracks contain continuous encoded audio rather than filesystems.
CUE/BIN, CCD/IMG, and MDS/MDF can store complete multi-track images with companion track metadata.
Historically, writing ISO to flash drives was limited by software tooling; raw-image writers later existed.
ISO is used for emulation, virtual CD-ROMs for hypervisors, and OS installation media.

value.mechanism: The OS decides when applications receive CPU time and how much memory/resources they receive.
value.effect: Prevents a single application from monopolizing limited hardware and enables concurrent application execution.
value.conditions: Multiple applications contend for finite CPU and memory resources.
value.inverse_or_converse: Without allocation, one program could monopolize resources.

value.mechanism: The OS separates applications so errors and security vulnerabilities in one application are contained while communication remains possible.
value.effect: Improves reliability and security without eliminating application communication.
value.conditions: Isolation must coexist with controlled inter-application communication.
value.inverse_or_converse: Unrestricted sharing increases interference risk.

value.mechanism: OS interfaces hide hardware-access details such as physical memory behind standardized services/interfaces.
value.effect: Programmers can develop against OS abstractions rather than hardware-specific details.
value.conditions: Hardware differences remain beneath the abstraction.
value.inverse_or_converse: Bypassing abstractions increases hardware dependence.

value.mechanism: OS exposes reusable interfaces for networking, disks and other common facilities.
value.effect: Applications can run across different hardware without being rewritten for each hardware implementation.
value.conditions: Service set varies greatly between OS designs.
value.inverse_or_converse: Missing services can force applications to depend on hardware-specific implementations.

value.mechanism: Paging/segmentation let the kernel choose mappings and use disk/RAM as a larger logical memory space.
value.effect: A program can perceive a large continuous address space even when physical memory is scattered or limited.
value.conditions: Requires hardware support and OS memory-management mechanisms.
value.inverse_or_converse: Invalid/restricted addresses can trigger faults.

value.mechanism: Kernel-enforced protection separates applications/users and limits their resource authority.
value.effect: Errors remain isolated and malicious software has less power to compromise private data or monopolize resources.
value.conditions: Depends on hardware privilege/memory-protection mechanisms.
value.inverse_or_converse: Broken protection increases cross-process interference.

value.mechanism: Hardware checks user-mode software for legal instructions while kernel mode has unrestricted powers.
value.effect: Separates ordinary application execution from privileged OS control.
value.conditions: Requires processor support for privilege modes.
value.inverse_or_converse: Executing privileged operations from user mode is prevented or traps to the kernel.

value.mechanism: The kernel creates a process, assigns memory/resources/priority, loads its binary and starts execution.
value.effect: Turns an application program into a managed unit of execution.
value.conditions: Exact process model varies by OS.
value.inverse_or_converse: An application may also execute another application within the same process or via a separate thread in systems described.

value.mechanism: An interrupt changes CPU control flow to an interrupt service routine; state is saved and later restored.
value.effect: Allows the OS to react efficiently to hardware/software events.
value.conditions: Architecture-specific interrupt handling differs.
value.inverse_or_converse: No interrupt handling would prevent timely OS reaction to device/events.

value.mechanism: When a device completes I/O it can interrupt the running process/CPU and provide status information.
value.effect: The OS can resume or schedule the process associated with the completed I/O.
value.conditions: Uses interrupt handlers, process state and context switching.
value.inverse_or_converse: If completion is not handled, the waiting process cannot be resumed normally.

value.mechanism: The scheduler changes the running process by saving one process's CPU state and restoring another's.
value.effect: CPU time is shared among runnable processes.
value.conditions: Depends on saved CPU state such as registers and program counter.
value.inverse_or_converse: A context switch is unnecessary when no process change occurs.

value.mechanism: Hardware-supported segmentation or paging restricts which addresses a process may access.
value.effect: One process cannot normally overwrite another process's memory; invalid access triggers an interrupt/fault.
value.conditions: Requires hardware support such as an MMU.
value.inverse_or_converse: A faulty/malicious access can cause a segmentation violation and process termination.

value.mechanism: Protected registers define permitted address regions; invalid access causes an interrupt and re-entry into supervisor mode.
value.effect: The kernel regains control and can terminate the offending program.
value.conditions: The source describes segmentation violation as a common response.
value.inverse_or_converse: Valid access avoids the fault.

value.mechanism: When one job waits for I/O, another job can use the CPU; multiple jobs are held in memory with partitioning and safeguards.
value.effect: Improves CPU utilization while preventing one job from accessing another's memory.
value.conditions: Requires memory partitioning/protection.
value.inverse_or_converse: Without multiprogramming, I/O wait would leave CPU less utilized.

value.mechanism: IEEE POSIX standardizes OS application-programming interfaces supported by most UNIX systems.
value.effect: Applications gain a common API target across compatible UNIX systems.
value.conditions: POSIX is an API compatibility standard, not an operating system.
value.inverse_or_converse: Nonstandard APIs reduce portability.

value.mechanism: OS services are provided as libraries and composed with one application/configuration code into a specialized single-address-space image.
value.effect: Avoids usual context-switch overhead and can deploy a minimal machine image.
value.conditions: Single application means traditional inter-application protection domains are unnecessary in the described model.
value.inverse_or_converse: More conventional OS boundaries reintroduce mode/context-switch overhead.

value.mechanism: Mode switching can pollute important processor structures including caches and the instruction pipeline.

OS vs kernel
value.description: Kernel is the always-running core; an OS can include system programs and other software beyond the kernel.

value.label: OS vs application
value.description: OS provides resource management/services; applications are other software running on the computer.

value.label: OS abstraction vs direct hardware execution
value.description: Application code generally executes directly on hardware but requests OS services and follows OS rules for privileged/hardware operations.

value.label: Multiprocessor vs multicomputer
value.description: Multiprocessors share memory; multicomputers have multiple CPUs with separate memory.

value.label: Multicomputer vs distributed system
value.description: Multicomputers are tightly coupled CPU/memory systems; distributed systems are distinct networked computers potentially dispersed worldwide.

value.label: Middleware vs OS
value.description: Middleware can function similarly to an OS but is an additional layer and not a true OS.

value.label: Embedded vs general purpose
value.description: Embedded systems may omit user-application protection because they do not load user-installed software.

value.label: Hard vs soft real-time
value.description: Hard real-time requires exact timing; soft real-time tolerates occasional missed events.

value.label: Hypervisor vs VM
value.description: The source describes the hypervisor as running a VM, while the VM is the application that emulates hardware.

value.label: Library OS vs conventional OS
value.description: libOS provides OS services as libraries composed with an application, reducing protection/context-switch overhead in the described single-application model.

value.label: User mode vs kernel mode
value.description: User mode is hardware-restricted; kernel mode has unrestricted OS privilege.

value.label: Hardware vs software interrupt
value.description: Hardware interrupt reports an event to the CPU; software interrupt communicates an event to a process/change of execution.

value.label: Interrupt vs signal
value.description: Signals are Unix-like process notifications analogous to software/hardware interrupt behavior but are an OS process communication mechanism.

value.label: Segmentation vs paging
value.description: Both provide memory protection, but they are distinct address-management mechanisms requiring hardware support.

value.label: Virtual memory vs physical memory
value.description: Virtual memory presents a logical address space whose backing can span RAM and disk rather than exposing physical layout directly.

value.label: Context switch vs interrupt
value.description: An interrupt can cause a context switch, but an interrupt is the event/control-transfer mechanism whereas a context switch changes the running process.

value.label: Resource allocation vs isolation
value.description: Allocation shares finite resources; isolation prevents one application's errors/authority from interfering with others.

value.label: Portability vs abstraction
value.description: Hardware abstraction and common OS services let applications run across different hardware without rewriting hardware-specific access.

value.label: UNIX vs POSIX
value.description: UNIX is an OS family/history; POSIX is an API standard for compatibility.

value.label: Linux vs Android
value.description: Android is closely based on Linux but uses a distinct user-space stack including Bionic and substantial Java code.

value.label: GUI vs CLI
value.description: GUI provides graphical interaction; CLI is text-based command interaction.

value.label: Preemptive vs cooperative behavior
value.description: Preemptive multitasking lets the OS scheduler interrupt/reassign CPU execution rather than relying entirely on voluntary cooperation.

value.label: System call vs library call
value.description: System calls request kernel services; libOS services can be accessed through simple library calls without usual context switches.

value.label: Protection vs no protection
value.description: Some specialized OS designs deliberately omit conventional application protection when their workload model makes it unnecessary.

value.statement: An operating system is just the kernel.
value.correction: The source explicitly distinguishes the kernel from system programs and applications; an OS can include software beyond the kernel.

value.statement: Applications never execute directly on hardware.
value.correction: The source says application code is usually executed directly by hardware while interacting with OS services through calls/interrupts.

value.statement: OS abstraction means hardware is irrelevant.
value.correction: The OS abstracts hardware details, but the kernel, drivers and hardware privilege mechanisms still mediate execution.

value.statement: Multicomputer and multiprocessor mean the same thing.
value.correction: Multiprocessors share memory; multicomputers have separate memory per CPU.

value.statement: A distributed system is one giant computer.
value.correction: The source describes distinct networked computers, potentially dispersed worldwide, each with its own OS/filesystem.

value.statement: All operating systems require full application isolation.
value.correction: Embedded and some hard-real-time/library OS designs may omit protection between applications under their workload assumptions.
Real-time is defined by timing guarantees/deadlines; hard real-time requires exact timing, not simply high throughput.

value.statement: A VM is the same thing as a hypervisor.
value.correction: The source distinguishes the hypervisor from the VM it runs.

value.statement: Virtual memory is the same as physical RAM.
value.correction: Virtual memory abstracts physical memory and can use scattered RAM and disk/backing storage.

value.statement: Every interrupt is a context switch.
value.correction: An interrupt can cause a context switch; the interrupt itself is the event/control-transfer mechanism.

value.statement: A software interrupt is a hardware interrupt.
value.correction: The source distinguishes software interrupts/messages to processes from hardware interrupts/messages to the CPU.

value.statement: POSIX is a UNIX operating system.
value.correction: POSIX is an API standard intended to increase compatibility among UNIX systems.

source_claims.statement: An operating system manages computer hardware/software resources and provides common services for computer programs.
Time-sharing OSes schedule tasks for efficient system use and may account for resource consumption.
OS acts as an intermediary for input/output and memory allocation while application code usually executes directly on hardware.
OS resource allocation shares CPU time/memory and prevents one program monopolizing limited hardware.
OS isolates applications to protect against errors/security vulnerabilities while enabling communication.
OS abstracts hardware access and virtualization can mask limited hardware resources.
OS common services for network/disk access enable applications to run across different hardware.
Multicomputers have multiple CPUs with separate memory and need efficient communication.
Distributed systems consist of distinct networked computers that may have their own OS/filesystem; middleware can improve consistency.
Embedded OSes target embedded systems and may omit application protection when no user-installed software is loaded.
Hard real-time systems require exact timing; soft real-time permits occasional missed events.
Hypervisors run VMs that emulate hardware and support OS research/development/debugging and portability.
Library OS services can be composed into a specialized single-address-space unikernel.
Early computers were directly programmed without OSes; operators manually performed scheduling/resource-management tasks.
OS/360 popularized multiprogramming and required memory partitioning and safeguards.
MULTICS targeted hundreds of simultaneous users; UNIX originated as a single-user development of MULTICS.
UNIX source availability led to System V and BSD; POSIX improved compatibility.
MINIX inspired Linux; MINIX later appeared in Intel microchip controllers.
CP/M was popular on early microcomputers; MS-DOS/IBM PC DOS became widespread on IBM PC compatibles.
Macintosh popularized GUI; Windows evolved from a GUI overlay to standalone Windows NT.
Android became a major mobile OS, using a Linux kernel and Bionic C library.
Kernel protects applications/users, manages memory, controls I/O, and separates user/kernel privilege.
Program execution typically creates a process, assigns resources/priority, loads binary code and starts execution.
Interrupts transfer control to an ISR and require saving/restoring execution state.
Software interrupts can represent normal timing, errors, user messages, and process communication.
Unix signals communicate asynchronous events; pipes coordinate producer/consumer processes.
Memory protection uses hardware-supported segmentation/paging; invalid access can trigger a segmentation violation.
Virtual memory can map scattered RAM/disk storage into a logical continuous address space.
Windows uses NTFS, Windows Driver Model, demand paging, preemptive scheduling, ACLs, integrity levels, authentication tokens and security descriptors.
Linux is distributed under GPL, uses a kernel/libraries/utilities structure, supports UNIX networking and preemptive multitasking, and can operate from small systems to large multiprocessors.

semantic_distinctions.label: OS vs kernel
semantic_distinctions.description: Kernel is the always-running core; an OS can include system programs and other software beyond the kernel.

semantic_distinctions.label: OS vs application
semantic_distinctions.description: OS provides resource management/services; applications are other software running on the computer.

semantic_distinctions.label: OS abstraction vs direct hardware execution
semantic_distinctions.description: Application code generally executes directly on hardware but requests OS services and follows OS rules for privileged/hardware operations.

semantic_distinctions.label: Multiprocessor vs multicomputer
semantic_distinctions.description: Multiprocessors share memory; multicomputers have multiple CPUs with separate memory.

semantic_distinctions.label: Multicomputer vs distributed system
semantic_distinctions.description: Multicomputers are tightly coupled CPU/memory systems; distributed systems are distinct networked computers potentially dispersed worldwide.

semantic_distinctions.label: Middleware vs OS
semantic_distinctions.description: Middleware can function similarly to an OS but is an additional layer and not a true OS.

semantic_distinctions.label: Embedded vs general purpose
semantic_distinctions.description: Embedded systems may omit user-application protection because they do not load user-installed software.

semantic_distinctions.label: Hard vs soft real-time
semantic_distinctions.description: Hard real-time requires exact timing; soft real-time tolerates occasional missed events.

semantic_distinctions.label: Hypervisor vs VM
semantic_distinctions.description: The source describes the hypervisor as running a VM, while the VM is the application that emulates hardware.

semantic_distinctions.label: Library OS vs conventional OS
semantic_distinctions.description: libOS provides OS services as libraries composed with an application, reducing protection/context-switch overhead in the described single-application model.

semantic_distinctions.label: User mode vs kernel mode
semantic_distinctions.description: User mode is hardware-restricted; kernel mode has unrestricted OS privilege.

semantic_distinctions.label: Hardware vs software interrupt
semantic_distinctions.description: Hardware interrupt reports an event to the CPU; software interrupt communicates an event to a process/change of execution.

semantic_distinctions.label: Interrupt vs signal
semantic_distinctions.description: Signals are Unix-like process notifications analogous to software/hardware interrupt behavior but are an OS process communication mechanism.

semantic_distinctions.label: Segmentation vs paging
semantic_distinctions.description: Both provide memory protection, but they are distinct address-management mechanisms requiring hardware support.

semantic_distinctions.label: Virtual memory vs physical memory
semantic_distinctions.description: Virtual memory presents a logical address space whose backing can span RAM and disk rather than exposing physical layout directly.

semantic_distinctions.label: Context switch vs interrupt
semantic_distinctions.description: An interrupt can cause a context switch, but an interrupt is the event/control-transfer mechanism whereas a context switch changes the running process.

semantic_distinctions.label: Resource allocation vs isolation
semantic_distinctions.description: Allocation shares finite resources; isolation prevents one application's errors/authority from interfering with others.

semantic_distinctions.label: Portability vs abstraction
semantic_distinctions.description: Hardware abstraction and common OS services let applications run across different hardware without rewriting hardware-specific access.

semantic_distinctions.label: UNIX vs POSIX
semantic_distinctions.description: UNIX is an OS family/history; POSIX is an API standard for compatibility.

semantic_distinctions.label: Linux vs Android
semantic_distinctions.description: Android is closely based on Linux but uses a distinct user-space stack including Bionic and substantial Java code.

semantic_distinctions.label: GUI vs CLI
semantic_distinctions.description: GUI provides graphical interaction; CLI is text-based command interaction.

semantic_distinctions.label: Preemptive vs cooperative behavior
semantic_distinctions.description: Preemptive multitasking lets the OS scheduler interrupt/reassign CPU execution rather than relying entirely on voluntary cooperation.

semantic_distinctions.label: System call vs library call
semantic_distinctions.description: System calls request kernel services; libOS services can be accessed through simple library calls without usual context switches.

semantic_distinctions.label: Protection vs no protection
semantic_distinctions.description: Some specialized OS designs deliberately omit conventional application protection when their workload model makes it unnecessary.

misconceptions.statement: An operating system is just the kernel.
misconceptions.correction: The source explicitly distinguishes the kernel from system programs and applications; an OS can include software beyond the kernel.

misconceptions.statement: Applications never execute directly on hardware.
misconceptions.correction: The source says application code is usually executed directly by hardware while interacting with OS services through calls/interrupts.

misconceptions.statement: OS abstraction means hardware is irrelevant.
misconceptions.correction: The OS abstracts hardware details, but the kernel, drivers and hardware privilege mechanisms still mediate execution.

misconceptions.statement: Multicomputer and multiprocessor mean the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Multiprocessors share memory; multicomputers have separate memory per CPU.

misconceptions.statement: A distributed system is one giant computer.
misconceptions.correction: The source describes distinct networked computers, potentially dispersed worldwide, each with its own OS/filesystem.

misconceptions.statement: All operating systems require full application isolation.
misconceptions.correction: Embedded and some hard-real-time/library OS designs may omit protection between applications under their workload assumptions.
Real-time is defined by timing guarantees/deadlines; hard real-time requires exact timing, not simply high throughput.

misconceptions.statement: A VM is the same thing as a hypervisor.
misconceptions.correction: The source distinguishes the hypervisor from the VM it runs.

misconceptions.statement: Virtual memory is the same as physical RAM.
misconceptions.correction: Virtual memory abstracts physical memory and can use scattered RAM and disk/backing storage.

misconceptions.statement: Every interrupt is a context switch.
misconceptions.correction: An interrupt can cause a context switch; the interrupt itself is the event/control-transfer mechanism.

misconceptions.statement: A software interrupt is a hardware interrupt.
misconceptions.correction: The source distinguishes software interrupts/messages to processes from hardware interrupts/messages to the CPU.

misconceptions.statement: POSIX is a UNIX operating system.
misconceptions.correction: POSIX is an API standard intended to increase compatibility among UNIX systems.
